why: Supply: hyperscalers retire many exabytes of DRAM per year; recovered bits cost ~5% of new-fab capex per bit and arrive in months.

title: Gen-8.5 display glass replaces 300 mm wafers for capacity memory
idea: Substitute DRAM fabs with idle LCD/OLED backplane lines: use their IGZO TFT process on 2.2x2.5 m glass to build 4-8 stacked layers of relaxed-pitch (~0.8 um) oxide-semiconductor gain-cell arrays, dice into large memory tiles with a bonded small CMOS controller, and sell as CXL far-memory modules.
why: Capital intensity and EUV (fact 4): depreciated display capex, zero EUV, new supply outside the DRAM-fab bottleneck; ~30-50 GB per layer per panel, roughly $8-15/GB at 4-8 layers, competitive at today's 4x prices for a slower ~100-300 ns tier.
note: Depreciated Gen-8.5 IGZO lines add EUV-free capacity; doubt: 0.8 um pitch density and slow tier may not hold $/GB long term.

title: CCD imager registers: vertical charge-shift strings replace capacitors
idea: Adapted from CCD image sensors: a 3D gate stack wrapped around a vertical silicon or oxide-semiconductor channel stores bits as charge packets in potential wells under each gate tier; a read clocks packets down the string to a floating-diffusion sense node at the base, like a CCD vertical register.
why: Removes both 3D blockers, the capacitor and the lateral transistor (fact 2); ~4F2/N per bit with NAND-like one-litho-for-all-tiers cost; trade-off ~50-100 ns serial shift for 32-tier strings.
note: NAND-like one-litho tiers with no capacitor; doubt: serial-only access, transfer losses, destructive string read.

title: Interposer-as-memory: oxide DRAM tiers in the passive interposer
idea: Under 400 C, build four oxide-channel 1T1C DRAM tiers in the BEOL of the large passive silicon interposer that already sits under the GPU and HBM, patterned with ArF at 40 nm. The interposer becomes about 100 GB of near memory directly under the compute die.
why: Facts 5 and 6: about 150 Mb per mm2 per tier on about 2500 mm2 of otherwise idle silicon, sub-pJ/bit access, no TSVs and no extra wafer.
note: Idle interposer BEOL becomes ~100 GB near memory at sub-pJ/bit; doubt: oxide 1T1C density at 40 nm and interposer cost.

title: All-IGZO monolithic memory: n-only periphery in the same tiers
idea: TRIZ #33 Homogeneity: build sense amps, decoders and drivers from the same IGZO transistors as the 2T0C array, using bootstrapped n-only (pseudo-CMOS) circuits, so each BEOL tier is a complete memory with no CMOS underneath. The whole stack can sit on any logic die's metal stack.
why: Fact 5 and 7: memory micrometres above compute (~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit HBM) and periphery needs no separate FEOL; any logic fab's BEOL becomes DRAM capacity.
note: Any logic BEOL becomes DRAM capacity; doubt: n-only IGZO sense amps are slow, variable and low-density.

title: Correlated double sampling sense amps read 0.2 fF cells
idea: Sample the bitline before and after charge sharing onto two capacitors in a logic-process sense amp and amplify the difference, cancelling offset and 1/f noise so the required signal approaches the sqrt(kT/C) floor instead of a 6-sigma mismatch margin.
why: First principles: sqrt(kT/C) for a 30 fF bitline is ~0.37 mV, so ~3 mV suffices versus ~80-100 mV today; Cs can fall from ~5 fF to ~0.2-0.5 fF, dissolving the charge wall (fact 1) and enabling lateral capacitors in 3D (fact 2).
note: CDS sense amp targets kT/C floor so Cs drops ~10x; doubt: WL/BL coupling and charge injection, not thermal noise, set the floor.

title: Overbuild 120 tiers, fuse to 100: tier-level sparing
idea: TRIZ #16 Partial or excessive action: deliberately deposit ~20% more tiers than the product needs, add a per-block tier-remap register, and e-fuse out any tier that fails test (shorts, Vt outliers, weak capacitors). The process window can then be loosened (faster deposition, cheaper precursors) because whole-tier defects become yield-neutral.
why: Fact 2: turns compounding tier loss (0.99^100 ~ 37% yield) into >90% die yield, cutting 3D cost per bit ~2x at a fixed defect density.

title: Core-rope via-programmed 3D weight store, one sense per rope
idea: Revive Apollo's core rope, where a bit was set by whether a wire threaded a core: inference weights are encoded by whether a BEOL via links a rope wire to a shared sense node, written by maskless laser/e-beam via patterning in a mature U.S. fab and stacked 16 metal decks high, with one sense amp per 64 rope wires. Static weights leave DRAM, which keeps only activations and KV cache.
why: Doing DRAM's job with less: weights are often >50% of inference DRAM; rope bits cost ~5-10x less than DRAM bits and need no EUV, capacitor or refresh.

title: HP's The Machine fixed: pooled memory racks with a refurbishment loop
idea: HPE's The Machine died betting on an unready memristor. Build the same memory-centric fabric with today's DRAM in CXL-attached pooled racks, sold as a service. Modules are hot-swapped, tested, refurbished and redeployed to lower tiers instead of retiring with the server.
why: Pooling cuts stranded DRAM (often 20-40% unused per server), and refurbishment roughly doubles module life, raising usable supply without new fabs.
note: CXL pooling widely pursued.

title: Memory on window glass: multi-tier oxide TFT cells on display lines
idea: Inverts 'memory is made on 300 mm silicon wafers': run 1T1C cells on idle Gen-8.5 to Gen-10.5 LCD/OLED glass lines, stacking 10-20 tiers with KrF-class litho at ~0.3 um and oxide-TFT access whose ultralow leakage lets tiny capacitors skip refresh; dice panels into tiles bonded to a small CMOS controller.
why: Display glass costs ~100-1000x less per area than leading-edge silicon; at 20 tiers and 4F2, ~$0.1-0.4/GB, ~25-100x cheaper; trade-off is ~100 ns-1 us access and lower density per volume.
note: Gen-10.5 glass is cheap per area; 20 tiers at 0.3 um could approach <$0.5/GB, but 100 ns-1 us access makes it capacity-tier, not DRAM.

title: Thousand-times-leakier cells tamed by a refresh engine per tile
idea: Inverts 'access transistors must leak <=13 fA': use the cheapest stackable access devices (unannealed sputtered poly-Si or oxide TFTs leaking ~10 pA) so retention is only ~10-100 us, and put a micro-sense-amp under each 4k-cell tile (CMOS-under-array) that refreshes its own tile continuously without touching global bitlines.
why: Trades refresh energy (~3-5x today) for ~100x lower cost per GB from low-temperature, 2-mask tiers with no deep capacitor; refresh traffic never leaves the tile, so bandwidth is unaffected.
note: Cheap stacked TFT tiers; doubt: 1000x refresh rate makes standby energy dominant.

title: Ephemeral RAM: leaky poly-Si cells for data that dies young
idea: IFR: the data dies before the bit does. Define an ephemeral memory class with 0.5-2 ms retention made of cheap, leaky poly-Si 2T0C gain cells stacked in NAND-style tiers, and have the accelerator runtime map only activations, gradients and KV blocks with measured lifetimes under a millisecond onto it, so refresh is never issued.
why: Constraint: accepting poor leakage buys NAND-like stacking cost, >10x density at about the same wafer cost, with zero refresh for the large short-lived share of accelerator traffic.
note: Accept ms retention to get cheap stacked poly-Si gain cells for short-lived AI data; doubt: 2T0C NAND-like stacking density claim.

title: Swap per-GPU weight copies for an optical weight-broadcast tree
idea: Substitute storage with broadcast. Instead of every accelerator keeping its own copy of the model weights in HBM, a central weight store streams each layer's weights over a WDM optical broadcast tree, timed to the synchronized decode step, so each of N accelerators buffers only the 1-2 layers in flight in SRAM. HBM is left for KV cache and activations.
why: Weights are copied 8-64x across a serving pod. One copy plus broadcast (~1.4 TB/s for a 70B fp8 model at 20 steps/s) cuts weight-resident HBM ~Nx, freeing 50-90% of HBM in weight-dominated serving. Attacks the HBM TSV tax and capital intensity.
note: One weight copy streamed per decode step frees most weight-resident HBM; doubt: ~1.4 TB/s optical receive per accelerator and strict lockstep.

title: Teletext data carousel: broadcast weights to accelerators that store nothing
idea: Borrowed from broadcast TV data carousels that loop content for any receiver to catch: a rack-level weight server streams the model layer by layer in a continuous optical multicast loop from ROM/NAND, and every accelerator computes on each layer as it passes, aligning its batches to the carousel phase.
why: N accelerators share one non-volatile copy of weights with zero weight DRAM and zero refresh; per-accelerator DRAM shrinks to KV only.
note: N accelerators share one streamed weight copy; doubt: batch-phase alignment and latency, Cerebras-style weight streaming partly known.

title: One latent per token regenerates every layer's K/V on demand
idea: Inverts 'each layer stores its own KV cache': DRAM holds a single low-rank latent per token (e.g., 256 dims), and each layer's tensor cores up-project it to K and V just in time inside the attention kernel, spending cheap FLOPs to save scarce bytes. A short distillation pass retrofits existing models so the shared cross-layer latent is trained jointly.
why: KV-cache bytes drop 10-40x vs per-layer FP16 KV, beyond per-layer latent attention, so long-context serving fits in a fraction of the HBM/DRAM.
note: 10-40x KV cut if one latent serves all layers; doubt: retrofit by short distillation; MLA/CLA partly there.

title: Minify embedding tables to hash encoders plus tiny MLPs
idea: Minify TB-scale recommender embedding tables into multi-hash encoders plus a small MLP that computes each embedding on the fly on tensor cores (deep hash embedding), with no stored rows.
why: Embedding memory falls 100x+, and recommender inference, a top consumer of server DRAM, needs >=10x less of it.
note: Embeddings computed not stored could cut recommender DRAM 10x+; DHE/TT-Rec prior art, doubt is compute cost and accuracy at scale.

title: Vinyl-record pressing: via-programmed mask ROM for frozen model weights
idea: Borrowed from record pressing, where one stamper makes millions of discs: frozen model weights are pressed into 1-transistor mask ROM by a single cheap via/metal mask on a commodity logic wafer (no EUV, no capacitor) stacked under the accelerator, so weights need zero DRAM and zero refresh; a new model version is a new via mask.
why: Removes the weight footprint from DRAM; mask ROM is dense, has zero standby and refresh power, uses mature U.S.-available nodes and needs no capacitor or EUV.

title: Minify replica count: consolidate long-tail models by global routing
idea: Minify how many places each model's weights must be resident: a global router concentrates all traffic for each long-tail model onto the fewest replicas that meet the SLO, and cold models page in from NVMe in under a second.
why: Pinned weight DRAM for fleets of thousands of models falls >=10x, which turns DRAM spend into a scheduling problem.
note: ServerlessLLM-style routing and fast loading known.

title: Minify graphs with gap-coded adjacency and hardware decoder
idea: Minify web and social graph adjacency using WebGraph-style reference copying, gap and zeta coding. A near-memory decoder streams neighbor lists at line rate to the graph engine.
why: Graph analytics needs 10-20x less memory per edge, so trillion-edge graphs fit in one rack.

title: Demoscene 64k coder: neural texture compression plugin for game engines
idea: Demosceners fit whole worlds in 64 KB. An Unreal/Godot plugin encodes each material's texture stack (albedo, normal, roughness and more) into a small latent grid plus a tiny MLP decoded in the shader at sample time, replacing block-compressed mip chains. A 4-person team can build it in 24 months.
why: Textures are 50-70% of game and VR memory. Neural textures give 4-8x over BCn, letting consoles, PCs and headsets ship with less DRAM.
note: NVIDIA NTC already exists; engine plugin is an execution play.

title: IBM MXT, fixed: compression moved behind CXL where latency is free
idea: MXT (2000) compressed all memory in 1 KB sectors behind a 32 MB L3, so every miss paid decompression and the extra cache chip cost more than the DRAM saved. Put an LZ4/zstd engine inside a CXL Type-3 expander that already costs ~150-250 ns, compress at 4 KB with a 64 MB uncompressed hot-line buffer, and expose 2-3x physical capacity as plain memory.
why: Cost per bit: 2-3x effective GB in the far tier; decompression hides inside the existing CXL hop, removing the latency and cost penalty that killed MXT.
note: Being commercialized (e.g. CXL compressed-memory controllers).

title: Host-DRAM-lite AI servers decode data shards directly on GPU
idea: IFR: AI-server host memory shrinks to almost nothing. Constraint: adding no new chips means adding no scarce elements, so delete host DRAM's jobs instead: compressed training shards go storage-to-GPU and are decoded by GPU kernels, and checkpoints stream GPU-to-NVMe directly, removing the staging buffers that justify 1-2 TB per node.
why: Host DRAM per AI node drops from ~2 TB to ~256 GB, an 8x cut on a large slice of server DRAM bought today.
note: GPUDirect Storage and GPU decode already exist.

title: Semantic snapshots: background apps keep only re-creatable state
idea: Imposed limit: a background phone app gets 2 MB. The OS makes each app serialize a semantic snapshot (navigation stack, form inputs, scroll positions, auth tokens) and then discards its heap; on relaunch the app rehydrates from the snapshot and a cached UI layout instead of restoring the whole heap.
why: Phones ship 12-16 GB mainly to keep apps warm; semantic snapshots could keep the same perceived warmth at 6-8 GB, and phones take roughly a third of all DRAM bits.
note: Android saved-instance-state already does this; adoption and perceived warmth are the hurdles.

title: Swap fp32 vector-index embeddings for 1-bit codes plus SSD rerank
idea: Substitute full-precision vectors in DRAM with sign-bit codes. Vector databases keep only binary codes in DRAM for Hamming-distance candidate search (popcount on existing CPUs) and read the fp32 vectors of the top ~100 candidates from NVMe to rerank.
why: Billion-vector RAG and search indexes shrink ~25x in DRAM at about a 1-point recall loss, with unchanged DDR.
note: Binary codes plus rerank already standard in vector DBs.

title: Swap greedy tensor allocators for ILP-planned rematerialization and packing
idea: Substitute runtime greedy allocation with a solved plan. One integer program over the training graph decides jointly which activations to keep, recompute or offload and their exact arena offsets, removing fragmentation and peak-coincident lifetimes before the run.
why: Training peak memory falls 2-4x versus caching allocators with heuristic checkpointing, for ~10-20% extra compute, on unchanged HBM.

title: Swap stored embedding rows for IDs hashed through a tiny MLP
idea: Substitute lookup with generation. Recommendation models replace multi-TB ID embedding tables with deep hash embeddings: k hash functions turn each ID into a dense code, a small shared MLP produces the embedding on the fly, and exact rows are kept only for the hottest 1% of IDs.
why: Embedding tables dominate recommendation DRAM, and generating rows cuts them 10-100x at small accuracy cost on unchanged servers.
note: Deep Hash Embedding is published prior art.

title: Datacenter-wide prompt-prefix KV cache on flash servers
idea: Combine content-addressed storage with LLM prefill: KV blocks for common prefixes (system prompts, documents, tool schemas) are hashed by token sequence and stored once on NAND-heavy cache servers, and inference GPUs fetch matching prefix blocks over RDMA instead of recomputing them or pinning them in HBM.
why: Deduplicates the large share of KV repeated across users, cutting per-GPU KV footprint and prefill compute, built entirely from DUV-made NAND and mature networking.
note: Mooncake, LMCache and CachedAttention already do this.

title: Minify vector-DB residency to 1-bit codes plus flash rerank
idea: Minify every resident embedding to a binary sign code (32x smaller than FP32). Candidates are found by popcount Hamming search in DRAM and reranked with full-precision vectors fetched from NVMe.
why: Vector databases hold 32x more vectors per GB of DRAM at near-equal recall.

title: Eliminate full fine-tune copies with 1-bit deltas over shared bases
idea: Store each fine-tuned variant as the sign of its weight delta plus per-row scales relative to one resident base model, served by a fused dequant-add GPU kernel; it is a software product.
why: Serving 100 variants needs about 1.1x base memory instead of 100x, a 10-16x saving per variant.

title: Snapshot-and-restore replaces warm serverless sandbox pools
idea: Reverse 'keep warm' into 'keep cold, restore fast': idle function sandboxes are snapshotted to NVMe and restored in ~5-10 ms by lazily faulting in only the pages the first invocation touches, instead of holding thousands of warm VMs in DRAM.
why: Warm pools often leave 50-80% of serverless DRAM idle; replacing them cuts that DRAM 3-5x in software alone.
note: Firecracker snapshots, REAP and FaaSnap already do this.

title: Cheap short-living objects: retired server DDR4 reborn as CXL memory
idea: TRIZ #27 Cheap short-living objects: hyperscalers retire millions of DDR4 DIMMs. Collect, retest and bin them, then mount 8-16 on each CXL Type-3 card built around a 28 nm controller, as a cheap cold tier for KV cache and page cache. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Usable supply: reuses DRAM that already exists, at ~10-20% of new DRAM cost per GB and zero wafer starts.

title: Piggy bank: retired DDR4 DIMMs reborn on CXL expander cards
idea: The 'piggy bank' of savings is the DDR4 sitting in decommissioned servers. Design a PCIe/CXL card around an off-the-shelf CXL memory controller ASIC that hosts 8 used DDR4 RDIMMs, plus a burn-in and test flow, and sell it as a capacity tier. Board design and pilot runs fit within $1M.
why: Cost per bit and supply: reused bits cost roughly 10-20% of new DDR5 and need zero new wafers.
note: Already deployed by hyperscalers (CXL DDR4 reuse); straightforward but not novel.

title: Ternary weights packed five trits per byte with LUT decode
idea: Box: representation shrink × model training × weights × train time × 3^5 = 243 states in 8 bits + table decode. Models trained natively ternary store five weights per byte and decode via a 256-entry table held in registers or shared memory.
why: 1.6 bits per weight versus 16 is a 10× weight-memory cut, achieved with algorithms and existing GPUs only, so no fluorinated chemistry.

title: Hashing-trick embedding tables at 1% size
idea: Worsen: keep a dedicated row for every user and item ID in TB-scale embedding tables. Flip: hash IDs into a table 100x smaller with multiple hash functions and train with collisions, adding a tiny per-ID sign or scale to separate colliding IDs.
why: Cost: 100x less DRAM for recommendation embeddings; trades small accuracy loss.

title: Keyword-spotter extreme: ternary weights stored as zero-skipping trit runs
idea: From always-on keyword spotters that run ternary networks: models are trained to {-1, 0, +1} weights stored as base-3 packed trits (5 per byte) with run-length skip lists for zeros, decoded by adder-only compute units that skip zero runs.
why: About 1.6 bits per weight or less versus 16 is a 10x+ cut in weight DRAM/HBM, and fab water falls proportionally.

title: Cobalt kobold miners: tiny SRAM index picks which KV pages to fetch
idea: Cobalt is named for the kobold that hunted ore; each 16-token KV page gets a 64-byte summary (per-channel key min/max) in SRAM, decode computes upper-bound attention scores from the summaries and fetches only the top 3-5% of pages from DRAM, while the rest of the KV lives in CXL memory or NAND.
why: Per-token KV traffic falls 20-30x (well over 10x lower energy per access), and the HBM/DRAM KV footprint shrinks to the hot pages with the long tail in cheaper flash (energy, cost/bit).

title: Datacenter-wide prefix radix tree deduplicates shared KV across users
idea: IFR: identical context is cached once for the planet. Closest with no materials: a cluster-wide radix tree keyed by token prefixes stores shared KV blocks (system prompts, popular documents, few-shot examples) once per pod, and requests are routed to the pod holding their longest prefix.
why: Shared prefixes are 30-70% of tokens in many products; that share of KV is deduplicated.

title: Cascade router sends easy queries to small models first
idea: IFR: every query is answered with the smallest memory possible. Closest with no hardware: a confidence-calibrated cascade routes queries to a 3B model (6 GB) first and escalates to the 400B model only when a verifier flags uncertainty, so fewer replicas of the giant model are needed.
why: If 70% of traffic stays small, giant-model replicas and their HBM drop ~3x.
note: FrugalGPT/RouteLLM are prior art.

title: SSD-controller playbook: 28nm CXL controller with page-level LDPC
idea: Adapted from NAND flash, which became cheap by pairing weak cells with smart controllers: a 28 nm CXL memory controller built in existing mature logic fabs applies 4 KB-codeword LDPC, with an on-chip SRAM write-combining buffer for read-modify-write, to unmodified commodity or lower-grade DRAM, exposing a byte-addressable device that tolerates raw BER ~1e-4.
why: Supply and cost per bit (facts 3, 4): operators can buy dies that fail JEDEC retention or speed bins at deep discounts and run them at 4-8x longer refresh; costs ~3% parity and ~50-100 ns added latency, acceptable for a CXL tier, with zero new fab capacity.

title: Proof-of-work logic: speculative-decoding drafts run from junk DRAM
idea: Crypto miners shrug off memory errors because every result is cheaply verified. Host LLM speculative-decoding draft models and their caches on retention-reject or relaxed-refresh DIMMs: the full model's verification pass rejects any token a memory error corrupted, so the only cost is a slightly lower acceptance rate.
why: Creates a productive market for weak-bin DRAM (several percent of output) and frees premium HBM for the target model (fact 3).
note: Clever verification-masks-errors insight, but the draft-model memory market is small.

title: H-free sputtered-Si laser grains as in-stack CMOS and floating-body tiers
idea: Sputter amorphous Si at ~100 C (no PECVD hydrogen) over ~0.5-1 um of SiO2 that carries a lattice of small grain-filter holes, then melt it with an excimer-laser pulse: the mu-Czochralski process grows one location-controlled single-crystal grain (3-7.5 um) from each hole, with electron/hole mobilities of 460-510 / 121-250 cm2/Vs reported by the Delft group. The ~100 ns pulse heats only the top ~0.3 um, so oxide tiers below stay cool. Use the grains for (a) complementary sense amps and decoders inside the stack, without Smart Cut's hydrogen implant (B3-09's main risk), and (b) floating-body capacitor-less 1T cells, which need holes and therefore cannot be made in n-type IGZO, for Ge-free 3D silicon DRAM tiers.
why: In-stack p-FET drive 8-17x that of a p-type oxide TFT with zero implanted hydrogen; Ge-free, epi-free floating-body tiers (1-beta parity at ~17 tiers, 1 bit).

title: ECC-paid capacitor: let the code, not the capacitor, carry the last 4 sigma
idea: Today's ~50 mV sense budget exists so that every one of ~1.7e10 cells reads correctly at ~7 sigma of sense-amp (SA) offset and coupling noise, with only on-die SEC as backup. Re-centre the array on a raw BER target of 1e-4 per read. A t=8 BCH code (80 check bits per 512 data bits) in the memory controller or HBM/CXL logic base die absorbs the errors; optionally the SA fires two extra comparator thresholds to hand one soft-information bit per cell to a NAND-style soft decoder. With dV_min of 26 mV instead of 50 mV, the ZrO2/TiN pillar storage node can hold ~2.7 fF instead of 5.4 fF on the same 512-cell bitline: ~640 nm tall instead of 1,300 nm. An SA's offset is static, so codewords run along the row (each bit through a different SA), and outlier SAs are fused out at test like today's column repair. The same rule gives a 0.6 fF cell on a 64-cell local bitline in a 3D tier.
why: Capacitor height 2.0x lower (1,300 -> ~640 nm, aspect ratio 62 -> 30) at a 1e-4 raw BER, or 2.5x lower (-> ~525 nm, AR 25) at 1e-3, for +9 to +21 points of check bits (15.6-27.3% vs DDR5's 6.25%). 3D or local-bitline tiers need only 0.5-0.6 fF instead of 1.2 fF.

title: Compression-funded ECC: compressible rows earn slow refresh for free
idea: On write, the controller compresses each line: exponent Huffman for float tensors, base-delta-immediate or zero-run for integers and pointers. If the result is <=54 B, it appends 70 parity bits (t=7 BCH over GF(2^10)) in the same 64 B slot and sets a mode bit in the existing ECC/metadata side-band. A per-row counter tracks whether every line in the row is in 'strong' mode; strong rows move to a slow refresh bin (RAIDR-style Bloom filter) and weak rows stay at 64 ms. A line that becomes incompressible demotes its row immediately, the safe direction. Reads run the full decode only when the cheap syndrome is nonzero.
why: 8-16x lower refresh energy (0.5-1 s interval) on fully compressible rows at zero capacity overhead. Float tensors compress to ~44 B per line, so this covers most of an AI accelerator's DRAM.

title: Top-k KV from in-memory scoring of MSB-plane sketches
idea: Keys are quantised per channel to INT8 (KIVI-style) and stored as bit planes. The 4 MSB planes live in a PIM-capable tier (HBM-PIM or LPDDR5X-PIM). The low planes and V live in a cheaper capacity tier (LPDDR or CXL DRAM). Each decode step broadcasts the query to bank-level units, which compute approximate q.k scores from the MSB planes with bit-serial adds at the sense-amp stripe or the existing PIM MAC units, and return only scores (2 B per token per KV head). The GPU picks the top-k tokens (k ~ 1-4k) and fetches their full K and V. Nothing is stored twice: the sketch is the high planes of the real data.
why: At 128k-token contexts: ~7x less KV traffic per decode step and ~8x less HBM capacity for KV, with full KV in a ~3x cheaper-per-bit tier. In-memory scoring cuts the sketch pass's interface traffic ~2,500x.

title: Thermal arbitrage: keep the bits away from the GPU's heat
idea: HBM sits millimetres from a ~1 kW GPU at 85-95 C (32 ms refresh above 85 C), and server DIMMs run 50-85 C. In a disaggregated design, capacity DRAM (KV pools, cold weights, CXL expanders) moves onto separately liquid-cooled sleds at 30-40 C, linked by optics (B4-14) or CXL. Refresh is set from on-die temperature and canary readings (B4-02), not the 85 C worst case. The cool margin can be spent three ways: (a) 4-30x longer refresh intervals; (b) multi-level rows (B4-05), whose droop budget is a third of single-level; (c) next-generation dies designed to a 'cool spec' with ~30% shorter capacitors.
why: Retention x3.7-18 from 85 C to 35 C (Arrhenius, Ea 0.25-0.55 eV; x32 by the 2x/10 C rule), so refresh energy and busy time fall 4-18x; or Cs 5.4 -> ~3.8 fF (the sense-limited floor), a ~30% shorter pillar.

title: Advance market commitment for next-generation memory bits
idea: Combine the vaccine Advance Market Commitment model with memory. Governments and hyperscalers pre-commit to buy the first 10 EB of any DRAM-class technology that meets $/GB, latency and endurance thresholds, at a guaranteed premium price that tapers.
why: Removes the demand-risk valley of death for 3D DRAM, gain-cell or capacitorless entrants. That pulls new tech and new fabs forward by years.
note: AMC model applied to new memory tech; addresses entrant demand-risk valley.

title: Magnify supplier count 10x with open-source DRAM IP
idea: Fund a DARPA-style open, royalty-free gain-cell memory macro, controller RTL and process module portable to any 22-40 nm logic fab, with qualified PDK decks for GlobalFoundries, TI, SkyWater-class and Intel 16, so ~30 mature logic fabs can make DRAM-class memory chiplets.
why: Breaks the 3-supplier oligopoly and the 1-2% U.S. share; taps idle mature-node capacity for capacity-tier memory without new fabs.
note: Open gain-cell macro on open PDKs is MPW-demonstrable; density well below commodity limits it to capacity/edge tiers.

title: Magnify sharing: rack-wide content-addressed memory deduplication
idea: A CXL memory fabric hashes every 4 KB page and keeps one physical copy rack-wide of identical model weights, container images, libraries and zero pages with copy-on-write, so inference fleets running one model on 64-128 accelerators share a single copy.
why: For weight-dominated AI fleets, usable GB per physical GB rises ~50-100x, cutting effective cost per usable GB ~100x.
note: 100x claim overstated: accelerator weights live in HBM, so dedup only helps host/pooled DRAM.

title: RISC-V-style royalty-free DRAM patent pool and periphery generator
idea: Like RISC-V plus the MPEG-LA patent pool, a foundation assembles expired 6F2/8F2 cell, sense-amp and DLL patents with donated ones into a royalty-free pool and ships an open-source periphery compiler that generates JEDEC-compliant row/column logic for a given process.
why: Lowers the IP and design entry barrier (often $0.5-1B and years) for new DRAM makers, especially U.S. and allied entrants.
note: Open DRAM periphery compiler (OpenRAM analog) is demoable in software.

title: Core-Rope ROM for Frozen Model Weights in Mature Fabs
idea: Revive Apollo's core rope memory, where the program was woven into the hardware: frozen foundation-model weights are written into via-programmed multi-level ROM chiplets (one custom via mask per model on a 28-40 nm mature line), read with small-swing sensing and no refresh or row restore, stacked beside the accelerator.
why: Energy per access ~10x lower than DRAM (~0.3 pJ/bit, no activation, restore or refresh); frees the large share of inference DRAM that only holds static weights, using mature-fab capacity.
note: Via-ROM at 28-40 nm is far less dense than DRAM and model churn needs a new mask per model.

title: Error-Tolerant DRAM grade: JEDEC spec permitting 1% raw cell errors
idea: Inverts 'every bit must work as shipped': a new JEDEC grade allows up to 1% faulty cells, with a boot-time defect map plus stuck-at masking codes for static faults and a rate-0.85 LDPC for random ones in the controller, sold as a cheaper price tier.
why: Cost per bit and supply: die now binned out for tiny fault counts become saleable; static faults cost only ~1-3% overhead with known-location coding, so good bits per wafer may rise 10-25%.

title: Phone LPDDR packages reballed onto CXL bridge cards
idea: Po: every phone is a memory mine. Recyclers desolder LPDDR4X/5 packages from end-of-life phones (hot-gas rework plus automated reballing), test them on a fixture, and mount 16-32 of them on a CXL Type-3 card whose controller bridges the LPDDR protocol and masks per-package defects with a remap table.
why: >1B phones a year reach end of life holding 4-12 GB each; recovering even 10% yields billions of GB of capacity-tier memory for cold pages with zero wafer starts; attacks cost per bit and scarce capacity.
note: Phone LPDDR reballed behind CXL bridge; testing/reliability cost decides economics.

title: Fiber-drawn salami capacitor arrays sliced into wafers
idea: Imposed scarcity: no lithography and no high-AR etch. Assemble a glass preform of millimetre metal-cored, glass-clad coaxial rods, thermally draw and restack-redraw it (as photonic-crystal fiber makers do) until cores reach ~50 nm pitch, then slice the fused bundle into 5 um discs and hybrid-bond them to a CMOS access-transistor wafer.
why: Feature size comes from draw ratio, not EUV; each slice is a sheet of billions of coaxial capacitors with AR ~100 at no etch cost, made from glass and common metals.
note: Pitch from draw ratio, no litho/etch; doubt: draw disorder breaks registration to access transistors and glass dielectric gives low Cs.

title: Hydrogen backside cooling shares the fab forming-gas recycle loop
idea: Combine the chuck's backside-cooling gas with the fab's existing H2 supply: run 5-15 Torr H2 (thermal conductivity ~0.18 W/m-K vs He ~0.15) under wafers in etch/CVD, recapture it through a palladium-membrane purifier and return it to the forming-gas anneal header.
why: Eliminates the largest in-fab helium use while Qatar's ~30% is offline; equal or better heat transfer; H2 can be electrolyzed on site in the U.S.
note: H2 conducts as well as He; plasma-side hydrogen effects and safety qualification are the work.

title: Eliminate writability for frozen weights: via-programmed 3D ROM replaces DRAM
idea: Encode a deployed model's weights as present/absent vias in 4-8 stacked metal layers written by maskless e-beam on mature-node wafers, read by low-swing sensing with no refresh or capacitor, with only activations kept in DRAM.
why: Weights are ~50% of inference memory; ROM reads at ~0.05 pJ/bit with zero refresh and frees DRAM supply, using no EUV or high-AR capacitor.
note: Via-programmed ROM for frozen weights; hardwired-model chips exist; e-beam write throughput for big models is a doubt.

title: Ephemeral memory: data dies before charge does, so never refresh
idea: Inverts 'stored data must outlive cell retention': a refresh-less DRAM tier holds only AI activations, gradients, KV blocks and packet buffers whose lifetime the compiler/runtime proves is below a guaranteed 10-50 ms retention, with hardware write-timestamps that fault any read past the deadline.
why: Zero refresh power in that tier; cells can use ~30:1 instead of 70:1 capacitors, roughly halving mold, fluorocarbon etch gas and ALD precursor per bit, and refresh counters vanish from the periphery.
note: Compiler-proved short data lifetimes enable refresh-free tier and shorter capacitors; weak-cell tail must still meet guarantee.

title: Socketed design-for-disassembly DRAM packages for multi-life reuse
idea: Box [standard die | standard | standard | compression-interposer LGA packages on CAMM/CXL boards | n/a | solderless assembly]: standardize DRAM packages that mount without solder and carry an on-package wear/retention log, so dies move from retired boards to new controller generations.
why: Raises usable supply per fabbed bit: stretching DRAM service life from ~5 to ~10 years through reuse could halve new-bit demand for capacity tiers, with no solder-rework yield loss.

title: Zero-helium wafer cooling with low-pressure hydrogen backside gas
idea: Ideal: etch/deposition chucks that need no helium. Closest achievable: run electrostatic-chuck backside cooling on 5-15 Torr H2 (thermal conductivity 0.18 vs 0.15 W/m-K for He) from on-site PEM electrolysis, with flow-limiting orifices and an N2-purged plenum so any leak stays below the flammability limit after exhaust dilution.
why: Helium: Qatar ~30% of supply offline since March 2026; backside cooling and purge are the dominant fab He uses. Removes ~60-80% of fab helium demand at equal heat transfer, using U.S.-made hydrogen.
note: Low-pressure accommodation coefficient and H2 safety/process interaction.

title: Eliminate low-order bits until needed: MSB-first bit-plane fetch
idea: Store tensors bit-plane transposed across sub-rows so the controller fetches the top 2-4 bit planes first; attention screening or early-exit logic requests the lower planes only for the ~5-10% of values that matter.
why: KV-cache attention moves ~8-12x fewer bits for the same answer, cutting energy per useful value and effective capacity demand.

title: Movable-type memory: one standard storage-element socket, swappable bit physics
idea: Like Gutenberg's interchangeable type in one press, define an open hybrid-bond 'socket': a fixed periphery and sense wafer with a standard 0.5 um-pitch bond pad per sub-array plus fixed voltage, timing and signal windows. Any new storage-element wafer (capacitor, ferroelectric, magnetic) bonds on and is tested with no periphery redesign.
why: Fact 7 and capital intensity: a new bit physics becomes a wafer swap rather than a $1B program. Trial cost drops ~10-50x and the periphery stays on a mature node.
note: Open periphery socket lowers trial cost for new bit physics; adoption is the question.

title: Short-retention cells matched to ephemeral AI tensors
idea: Combine compiler-known tensor lifetimes with deliberately cheap short-retention cells: activations, KV-cache pages and gradients that are overwritten within 50 ms go to a pool whose cells retain only ~100 ms worst case and are never refreshed. A runtime time-to-live tag per page rewrites or evicts data before expiry, so refresh disappears and the capacitor can be ~3x smaller.
why: Zero refresh power for the AI-dominant data class, and a smaller Cs (fact 1) allows lower AR and a cheaper process.
note: Compiler TTL plus unrefreshed short-retention pool; provable on FPGA with refresh disabled.

title: Eliminate the 64-ms retention spec: ephemeral sub-femtofarad cells for transient tensors
idea: Eliminate the assumption that every bit must survive 64 ms: build a memory class whose storage node is a planar ~0.5 fF capacitor with no pillar and ~100 us retention, used only for AI activations, KV-cache spill and gradients that are overwritten within microseconds; the controller tags allocations by lifetime and never refreshes them.
why: Removes the AR 60-75 pillar (facts 1, 4) for a large share of AI traffic; ~2-3x cheaper per bit for the ephemeral tier with zero refresh energy (fact 3).
note: Lifetime-matched no-refresh tier for AI transients; similar to refresh-skipping eDRAM for DNNs.

title: Shallow 1 fF pillars rescued by soft-decision sensing and LDPC
idea: Invert 'every cell must read correctly on its own' -> let cells be weak and the code be smart. Etch only 1 fF, AR ~15 pillars; sense amps emit 2-bit soft information (strong/weak 0/1) to an on-die LDPC decoder over 512-bit codewords, tolerating raw BER ~1e-3 that would kill a hard-decision chip.
why: Cuts capacitor AR 4-5x (fact 1) and lets refresh stretch since weak cells become erasures (fact 3), for ~12% parity plus decoder area; decoder latency is the risk.
note: LDPC soft sensing trades capacitor AR for decoder; latency is the doubt.

title: Bootstrapped T-switch gain cell zeroes leakage across its write path
idea: TRIZ #12 Equipotentiality + #25 Self-service: write the gain-cell storage node through two series transistors and drive their middle node from the cell's own source-follower output, the guard trick from electrometers and sample-and-hold circuits. The inner transistor then sees ~0 V drain-source, so subthreshold leakage collapses.
why: Fact 3: leakage down ~50-100x, stretching refresh from 64 ms to seconds with plain Si or oxide transistors.
note: Known guard/T-switch trick; demoable on MPW, area penalty limits value to eDRAM.

title: Seed-regenerated tensors replace stored bits with recomputation
idea: Time-shift storage into computation: store a 32-bit PRNG seed plus a few coefficients per weight block, and regenerate weights on the fly in a near-memory generator at read time, so the bit lives as an algorithm.
why: DRAM demand: 3-8x fewer bits stored for compressible model weights, which raises usable supply without fabs.
note: Close to SeedLM-style PRNG weight compression; accuracy loss limits ratio.

title: Matchstick: consume-once reads with decoupled sense amps skip restore
idea: A match is used once: add an isolation gate so the SA latches from a +/-100 mV bitline signal without driving the bitline rail to rail, and add a READ-CONSUME command; for data the host marks read-once (streamed KV cache, network buffers, transpose scratch) the row is left destroyed and marked free, so neither full swing nor restore happens.
why: Full-swing restore is >70% of activation energy; consume reads cut array energy ~10x and halve tRAS; needs a JEDEC/CXL command and OS tracking of dead rows.

title: Self-service: read-write-read self-reference removes matched sense amp pairs
idea: TRIZ #25 Self-service: each read samples the bitline after charge sharing, writes a known '1', shares again and samples a second time, comparing the cell with itself on one capacitor pair; device mismatch, reference bitlines and dummy cells cancel, so sloppy TFT or 180 nm transistors can serve as the sense amp.
why: 100x path: sensing works with ~100 mV-offset cheap devices and single-ended bitlines on mature or TFT lines; trade-offs: ~3x longer read cycle and an extra write per read (energy and disturb). Attacks Facts 4 and 7.

title: Potluck cookbook: open-source, silicon-proven DRAM periphery IP commons
idea: A potluck works because everyone shares recipes. Fund an open-source library of DRAM periphery blocks (sense amps with offset calibration, row-hammer trackers, pumps, LPDDR/DDR5 PHYs) with silicon-proven layouts on U.S. 28/22 nm processes, so startups and foundries can build memory dies without decades of trade-secret circuit know-how.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: periphery know-how is a hidden entry barrier; shared IP could cut a new entrant's design cost from ~$500M to ~$50-100M and save ~2 years.

title: Venetian blinds: bit-plane layout fetches only requested precision bits
idea: Tilt Venetian blinds to let in only the light you want. Store tensors transposed into bit-planes across column groups, with a precision-select field in the column command so a 4-bit or 8-bit inference read opens only those planes' micro-rows and moves only those bits, not the full 16-bit words.
why: Activation plus transfer energy scales with bits actually needed: 2-4x from precision alone, and >10x when combined with micro-row activation that already removes overfetch.

title: Po: shrink the capacitor to amplify — MOS varactor parametric gain
idea: Po: an amplifier with no gain transistor. Sample the bitline differential onto a pair of silicon MOS varactors held in accumulation, then pulse them into depletion so their capacitance falls ~5x while charge is conserved, raising the differential voltage ~5x before the latch.
why: Capacitor wall (#1) and periphery (#7): ~5x voltage gain before any matched transistor, so SA offset matters ~5x less; silicon and oxide only.

title: Token-synchronous memory: decode sweeps restore every row each token
idea: Align the workload clock with the leakage clock: LLM decode reads all dense weights and active KV each token (~20-50 ms) and every DRAM read restores its row, so the refresh engine is removed from the die; a 1-bit-per-row coverage bitmap faults if any row goes unread for one retention window, and sparse MoE experts live in an NV tier.
why: Zero refresh power and 10-20% of bandwidth returned (fact 3); refresh counters and logic leave the periphery (fact 7).

title: Row-granular decompressor in the sense-amp stripe, after IBM MXT
idea: Failure mined: IBM's MXT compressed main memory died on decompression latency and a costly controller far from the DRAM. Fix: put a wide, row-granular decompressor (zero-run coding plus 4-bit quantization tables for AI weights, KV caches and activations) right after the secondary sense amps. Its work overlaps the activation's tRCD and rows are stored compressed, so effective capacity multiplies with no added latency.
why: 10x effective density at the same cost for AI data: 4:1 quantization x ~2.5:1 sparsity and zero-run coding = ~10x usable capacity per bit cell. It also cuts data-movement energy (fact 5) ~10x per useful value, for ~3% of die area.

title: IBM eDRAM trench sold as merchant pre-capacitored substrate wafers
idea: IBM's deep-trench eDRAM died when its single in-house SOI process ended with GlobalFoundries' 7 nm exit. Disaggregate it: a substrate vendor (Soitec-style) mass-produces blank wafers with a uniform grid of deep-trench capacitors, and any fab, including U.S. legacy logic fabs, builds access transistors and periphery on top aligned to that grid.
why: Capital: moves the deepest etch and high-k module into one specialized high-throughput substrate fab; lets non-memory fabs make DRAM-class memory; ~30% of DRAM process steps outsourced to a shared, fully utilized line.
note: Lets logic fabs build DRAM-class memory on a pre-made cap grid; density stays at eDRAM levels.

title: Substitute die-to-wafer bonding with micro-transfer-printed DRAM tiles on compute
idea: Release 0.5-1 mm2 DRAM tiles from their wafer by undercutting a sacrificial layer, pick thousands at once with an elastomer stamp, and print them directly over compute tiles on the processor wafer, followed by planarization and a via step for um-scale connections.
why: Constraint: tiles ~5 um above cores give ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit access (>=10x below HBM); capital: stamps place thousands of tiles per cycle with no hybrid-bond aligner or TSVs, and tiles can come from older fabs.

title: Vertical codewords across tiers break 3D DRAM yield compounding
idea: Combine 3D NAND-style tier stacking with tier-orthogonal coding: each codeword takes one symbol from each of ~32 tiers along the vertical bitline, so a defective tier (lateral-transistor shorts, capacitor voids) costs only one symbol per codeword. Per-tier yield can then be 99% rather than 99.99%.
why: Tier-yield compounding is a hidden blocker for 26+ tiers (fact 2). Relaxed per-tier yield permits faster deposition, fewer inspections and ~2x more tiers per stack.

title: Token-sweep restore: inference reads replace refresh, shortening capacitors
idea: TRIZ #25 Self-service: in LLM-inference memory every weight row is activated once per decode step (~10-16 ms) and each activation restores the cell, so the controller disables refresh and guarantees the sweep period; if serving pauses beyond the bound it drops the weights and reloads them from flash, keeping refresh power exactly zero.
why: Zero refresh power and bandwidth (16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth today); a guaranteed ~16 ms window vs 64 ms cuts required Cs ~3x, so capacitor AR falls from ~70:1 to ~25:1, deleting support-mesh masks and halving HAR etch time (facts 1, 3, 4).

title: Base-array mask ROM with one e-beam-written via layer
idea: TRIZ #10 Prior action: pre-build generic NOR-ROM wafers (4F2 transistor arrays, DUV plus SAQP, ~25 masks, no capacitor) in bulk; once a model is frozen, program its weights by e-beam direct-writing a single via layer with two via sizes per bit-pair (2 bits/cell), so inference weights live in silicon with zero refresh and zero standby.
why: Weights are most of inference memory; ROM cost per bit could be ~3-5x below DRAM (no HAR capacitors, no EUV, ~40% fewer masks), frees DRAM for KV and activations, and maskless customization avoids per-model mask sets (facts 3, 4).
note: No capacitor or refresh for frozen weights; model churn and e-beam throughput limit it.

title: Core-rope weights: maskless via-programmed BEOL ROM frees HBM
idea: Revive Apollo's core-rope memory, where the wiring itself encoded the program: build generic base wafers with 8 stacked metal crossbar levels and encode a frozen model's weights only in the via layers, written maskless by multibeam e-beam, so each model ships as a ROM chiplet. Weights leave DRAM; HBM keeps only activations and KV cache.
why: Doing DRAM's job with less: static weights are ~50-80% of inference memory; 4F2 per via level x 8 levels at 40 nm metal pitch is ~DRAM-class density with no capacitor, no refresh and no per-model mask set.

title: Laser interference gratings plus coarse cuts define the whole array
idea: Worse: insist that every array layer needs a $200M scanner and a custom reticle. Flip: expose the purely periodic wordline/bitline layers with maskless two-beam 193 nm immersion interference lithography (a ~$10-20M tool), pitch-split by SAQP, then trim with one low-resolution DUV cut mask. Arrays need periodicity, not arbitrary shapes.
why: Capital intensity: array litho tool cost drops ~10x and array masks shrink to cut layers only.

title: Federated defect-image library compresses new-fab yield ramps
idea: Worse: every new fab learns its defects alone over 2-3 years. Flip: entrants and toolmakers feed inline SEM/optical defect images and parametric fails into a standardized defect taxonomy. Classifiers train federated (data never leaves each fab) and ship root-cause models and recipe corrections to new lines on day one.
why: Capital: ramp months burn depreciation (~55% of wafer cost); cutting the ramp from ~24 to ~10 months saves ~$1B+ per new fab.

title: Datacenter fleets as ore: reverse-fab reclaim of retired DRAM dies
idea: Scale shift from fab to fleet: DIMMs retired after 4-6 years are laser/chemically decapped, dies are retested and rebinned, then re-assembled onto new substrates or CXL expander cards as capacity-tier memory with stronger ECC.
why: Adds bits with ~zero fab capex; a hyperscaler fleet could recover 30-60% of retired bits at <20% of new-die cost.

title: Open capacitorless memory macro qualified at every U.S. logic fab
idea: Ideal: every fab already in the country is a memory fab. Closest: a CHIPS-funded open PDK macro (gain-cell array, sense amps, refresh controller) qualified on Intel 18A, TSMC Arizona, GlobalFoundries and SkyWater flows, so any U.S. chip can carry hundreds of MB on-die and GB-class stacked working memory without a DRAM fab.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: zero new fab capex; turns logic wafer starts into memory supply and cuts off-chip DRAM demand for caches and KV buffers.

title: Display fabs build IGZO memory tiers on Gen-8.5 glass panels
idea: [Box: 2T0C gain charge | IGZO TFT | current sense | many-tier panel-level stack | 2.2 x 2.5 m glass | i-line/ArF dry steppers in existing LCD/OLED fabs] Use idle display-fab capacity to build IGZO gain-cell arrays at ~0.5 um F on huge glass panels, stack 8-16 tiers, and dice them into CXL capacity-tier memory modules.
why: Capital intensity and supply: at 8F2, F=0.5 um gives ~60 GB/m2 per tier, ~340 GB per panel tier; glass costs ~100x less per m2 than processed Si, with no EUV.
note: ~$5/GB per tier on glass: above DDR5 cost but below contract price, with no EUV.

title: Drum-era SOAP placement makes shift-register memories act random-access
idea: Revive the IBM 650's Symbolic Optimal Assembly Program, which placed each next instruction where the rotating drum would be when needed: a compiler/controller lays out tensors, KV-cache pages and weights in shift-register arrays (CCD strings, racetracks, delay loops) so the next word reaches the read port just in time, with out-of-order prefetch hiding the rest.
why: Lets transistor-free serial 3D arrays serve the predictable ~60-80% of AI memory traffic at effective 10-30 ns latency, unlocking 5-10x denser arrays for DRAM's job.

title: Weimer's 1962 TFT reborn: panel-fab memory on Gen-8 glass
idea: Revive RCA's thin-film transistor for memory: build 4-tier oxide-TFT DRAM-like arrays on Gen-8.5 glass in idle LCD and plasma panel fabs at ~1 um features, accept 1% defective cells across huge panels with block codes, and sell them as cheap capacity modules.
why: Capital intensity and U.S./allied manufacturability: panel fabs cost ~100x less per m2 than DRAM wafers; at 4 tiers cost could approach ~$10/GB with no EUV or quartz crucibles.

title: Matrix Semiconductor's write-once 3D ROM as a weights tier
idea: Matrix Semiconductor's 8-deck antifuse crosspoint (2001) failed because nobody wanted write-once storage. LLM inference does: burn model weights into a stack of antifuse decks over the accelerator's periphery, read in tens of ns. The weights no longer occupy DRAM, which then holds only KV cache and activations.
why: Does DRAM's job with less DRAM: weights are ~50-80% of inference memory, written once at ~10x DRAM's bits per mm2, with no refresh.
note: Hardwired weights offload DRAM; model churn limits value.

title: Minify rank width: one-chip sub-rank access controller
idea: Build an FPGA DIMM controller that addresses each x4 DDR5 chip independently through per-chip command buffering, so a random access activates one chip's row instead of 8-16 chips' rows.
why: Overfetch: random-access activation energy (graph, KV cache) could fall about 8x on existing DIMMs. The FPGA prototype costs about $250k.

title: Eliminate the incumbents' data monopoly: open 1-um access-device PDK across universities
idea: Publish an open process kit for 100 mm wafer access devices (Si, SiC, Ga2O3 variants) runnable in ten U.S. university nanofabs, each running monthly shuttles with standardized retention-tail test structures; pooled data on millions of cells reveal which elimination (junction, oxide, body) shrinks the tail.
why: Breaks the barrier that only three firms see leakage-tail statistics at scale; accelerates U.S. access-device innovation for ~$10M/yr instead of a $15B fab.

title: Unified charge-debt counter for retention and row hammer
idea: Each row carries one counter that accumulates time weighted by temperature plus neighbor activations weighted by coupling. A row is refreshed when its debt crosses a threshold, so one mechanism handles both retention and hammer.
why: Replaces the fixed 64 ms sweep plus separate TRR. Quiet rows refresh 4-8x less often, and hammer victims (fact 9, ~1k ACTs) are restored exactly in time.
note: Per-row counters cost area; neat merge of retention and TRR.

title: Banker's insured deposits: refresh-free banks for data with backups
idea: A banker guards insured deposits lightly because losses are covered. Pages with a valid copy elsewhere (model weights, page cache, read-only datasets) go into banks run with refresh off or at 1-4 s, protected by strong per-line detection codes; a detected error triggers a transparent refetch from flash, CXL or a remote replica instead of a crash.
why: Read-mostly AI weights are a large share of DRAM; dropping their refresh cuts refresh power and bandwidth 50-90% in those banks with only detection metadata added.
note: At 1-4 s many cells fail; refetch rate and detection overhead decide net gain.

title: Deep-space LDPC pages: refresh at the 1% retention quantile
idea: CCSDS deep-space links decode reliably near 1e-2 raw BER. Store each 4 KB page as one LDPC codeword (~15% parity, decoder in the HBM base die or CXL controller) and set refresh where 1% of cells have decayed instead of where the last 1e-9 tail cell does; the median retention distribution is far longer than the tail, so the interval grows from 64 ms to ~1-2 s.
why: Fact 3: refresh energy and bandwidth loss fall ~15-30x and per-row profiling and VRT guardbands are no longer needed; costs ~15% parity and decode latency hidden behind page-granular access.
note: Extends Hi-ECC ideas to LDPC at 1% BER; page-granular access and decode latency are costs.

title: Lossy NUMA node standard: OS pages tagged by error tolerance
idea: Push a JEDEC/CXL descriptor that publishes each region's raw-BER-vs-refresh curve, plus a Linux 'lossy NUMA node' reached with mmap(MAP_LOSSY). KV caches, media buffers and caches go to 1%-BER regions refreshed rarely; kernel and databases stay on fully protected memory.
why: Supply and fact 3: makes 1%-BER memory a standard, procurable class so the other tolerance tricks deploy across vendors; government AI-cluster procurement can require support.

title: Ten people, one kernel module: retire weak pages, run 4x tREFI
idea: 10-person constraint: ship software plus a BIOS setting. A kernel module runs a retention test at 4x the refresh interval and retires the ~0.01-0.1% of 4 KB pages that fail (BadRAM-style memmap exclusion). It stores the compressed failing-page list in the DIMM's user-writable SPD bytes so the list travels with the module, then sets tREFI 4x longer.
why: Fact 3: cuts refresh energy ~75% and recovers ~8-15% of bandwidth for under 0.1% of capacity, on any server, with no new hardware.
note: BadRAM plus longer tREFI; VRT and data-pattern dependence need guardband.

title: 2050 engineer: KV cache stored as per-sequence implicit neural field
idea: A 2050 engineer stores functions, not tables. For each long sequence, a tiny sinusoidal MLP per layer is fitted online to map (position, head) to the K/V vector and refitted incrementally every few hundred tokens, and attention queries this field instead of a table. Exact KV is kept only for the recent window and for outlier tokens the field reconstructs poorly.
why: KV cache dominates long-context inference memory. A 20-50x fit on older tokens would turn 1M-token contexts from hundreds of GB into a few GB. The accuracy risk is high.
note: KV as fitted implicit function could give 20-50x; doubt: K/V vectors are not smooth in position, so fits likely lossy.

title: Americium credit: U.S. tax credit per gigabyte of DRAM avoided
idea: Named for the Americas, a CHIPS-style federal credit pays data-center operators per GB-year of DRAM avoided against a certified baseline (via compression, pooling, reuse) measured by a standard telemetry audit, and federal procurement favors software that publishes bytes-per-transaction figures.
why: Makes memory efficiency a domestic supply lever while the U.S. makes only 1-2% of DRAM; a 15% demand cut equals several fabs' output without $15B of capital (capital, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Garbage collector fused with a columnar compressor for old generation
idea: Combine the generational GC's copying/promotion phase with compression: objects promoted to the old generation are packed into per-class columnar blocks (field-transposed, delta- and dictionary-encoded), and a read barrier decompresses on access through a small decoded-object cache.
why: Managed heaps (Java, Go, JS, Python) run at 2-5x live data with highly redundant fields; a 2-3x old-gen shrink is plausible.

title: Retired GPUs become attention-computing KV-cache servers
idea: Combine previous-generation accelerators (HBM2-era parts on non-EUV processes) with attention offload: the new GPU ships query vectors over the network, the retired GPU holds long-context KV in its HBM and returns attention outputs, so only small vectors cross the link.
why: Turns stranded HBM2 into extra KV capacity without new DRAM and frees 50-70% of new GPUs' HBM for weights and batch.

title: Video-codec P-frames: delta-encoded memory pages against reference pages
idea: Borrowed from MPEG inter-frame coding: a CXL memory-expander controller keeps 'I-pages' as references and stores near-duplicate pages (VM clones, forked workers, fine-tuned weight variants, beam-search KV copies) as XOR/byte-delta 'P-pages' with offset hints, decoded in a ~20 ns pipeline on read. A MinHash similarity index chooses each page's reference at write-back time.
why: Capacity/cost per bit: near-duplicate (not identical) pages are invisible to exact dedup; claims 2-6x effective capacity on multi-tenant and multi-variant model hosts.
note: Hardware Difference-Engine; near-duplicate pages via MinHash reference selection is a fair twist.

title: Magnify dictionaries: hardware zstd for in-memory logs and JSON
idea: Magnify compression context with trained multi-MB dictionaries per data type (logs, JSON, traces). A CXL-module decompressor at 50 GB/s serves reads, and the in-memory store keeps everything compressed.
why: Log, trace and JSON stores compress 10-20x with trained dictionaries, giving >=10x capacity on the same DIMMs.

title: Bit-plane progressive fetch stops when precision suffices
idea: Eliminate low-order bits from the bus: store tensors transposed into bit-planes and fetch sign/exponent/MSB planes first; the consumer's datapath signals 'enough' as soon as the result (e.g., top-k ordering or a dot-product bound) can no longer change, and the remaining planes are never sent.
why: Data movement is 20-25% of accelerator power: on LLM decode ~40-60% of mantissa bits are provably unnecessary per operation, cutting bytes moved ~1.5-2x without fixed quantization loss.
note: Exact early termination on bounds (top-k) is the non-obvious part; bit-plane layout costs write/compute overhead.

title: Memory-side top-k gate returns token indices, not keys
idea: Eliminate shipping full key vectors: each HBM pseudo-channel's base-die slice holds a small dot-product unit and comparator tree that scores the query against stored keys inside the stack and returns only the top-k token indices; only those value rows then cross the interface.
why: Long-context KV reads dominate decode bandwidth; for k=64 of 128k tokens interface traffic falls >10x for ~3-5% base-die area.

title: Via-ROM weight chiplet: frozen weights need no DRAM
idea: Eliminate DRAM, its writes and its refresh for deployed model weights: encode weights in a single custom via-mask layer of a mature-node ROM die (one via = one bit) hybrid-bonded under the compute die; the data survives power loss by construction.
why: Weights are ~60-80% of inference memory; via-ROM is ~5x cheaper per bit than DRAM, needs one 28-40 nm mask (no EUV, U.S.-fabbable) and reads at ~0.1 pJ/bit over hybrid bonds.
note: Mature-node via-ROM is ~10x less dense than DRAM; only frozen models; Taalas-like hardwiring exists.

title: Bit-plane-major storage with progressive-precision fetch
idea: Rearrange bit order: weights are stored transposed so that each DRAM burst holds the same bit position of 512 different weights. The accelerator fetches the top 4 bit-planes first and fetches lower planes only for layers or tokens whose error estimate needs them.
why: Facts 5 and 8: inference moves 2-4x fewer bytes on average at near-equal accuracy, multiplying effective bandwidth and turning precision into a runtime knob instead of a stored format.
note: Close to Any-Precision LLM bit-plane storage and bit-serial accelerators.

title: Transfer-print thin memory membranes, then wire them lithographically
idea: Reverse bond-then-connect: undercut-release memory chiplets into <10 um membranes, pick them with a PDMS stamp onto the logic wafer, planarize with BCB, and pattern vias and copper across both with ordinary lithography, giving a monolithic-like 2-3 um-pitch connection with no bumps.
why: Fact 5: interconnect density ~10x microbumps at ~0.05 pJ/bit, using university-standard transfer printing, spin coating and plating.

title: Train models with KV-dropout so memory starvation is harmless
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise: inject random KV eviction (drop 30-70% of past tokens' KV, biased toward older ones) as a regularizer during pre- and post-training, turning the harm of missing context into learned robustness so inference can evict aggressively with negligible quality loss.
why: KV eviction degrades unadapted models; evictability-trained models could run at 2-4x smaller KV budgets.

title: Buffet-line broadcast: one DRAM read feeds every accelerator
idea: One buffet tray serves every diner. Likewise, a weight-streaming memory node reads each weight block once and puts it on a shared multidrop optical/SerDes broadcast bus. All N data-parallel accelerators in the pod latch it at the same moment, in a synchronized schedule.
why: Data-parallel inference replicas all read the same weights. Broadcasting cuts DRAM reads and weight capacity N-fold: 8 replicas share one copy, freeing ~7/8 of weight HBM for KV cache.

title: OS lossy heap: applications declare error tolerance per allocation
idea: Inverts 'memory must be bit-exact': a new mmap flag (MAP_LOSSY plus an error bound) sends ML activations, image buffers and analytics sketches to a region where the memory controller applies error-bounded floating-point compression (ZFP/SZ-style) on writeback. Exactness stays the default; lossy bytes are opt-in and typed.
why: 3-8x effective capacity on tolerant data, which is often 30-60% of an ML or media server's footprint.

title: Rank/select engines enabling succinct trees and graphs in DRAM
idea: Information theory says an n-node tree needs only ~2n bits, yet pointer trees spend ~128n. Add rank/select and balanced-parentheses navigation units next to the memory controller so succinct encodings (LOUDS, BP, Elias-Fano adjacency lists) traverse in O(1) per hop at near-pointer speed.
why: 5-20x smaller indexes, tries, graphs and genomics structures, which are often DRAM-bound.

title: Twenty-millivolt bitline-style die-to-die links bounded by kT/C
idea: The true floor on signal swing is thermal noise sqrt(kT/C), ~0.2 mV rms on a 100 fF bonded link, so 20 mV still gives >10 sigma margin. Replace 0.4 V HBM drivers with charge-dump transmitters and cross-coupled latch receivers clocked like a DRAM sense amp (precharge, share, regenerate), with per-lane offset trim stored at boot.
why: Energy ~C*VDD*dV falls ~20x versus 0.4 V swing: HBM 3-4 pJ/bit toward ~0.2 pJ/bit (fact 5), and smaller I/O cells shrink periphery (fact 7).

title: Twin synchronized predictors send only the surprise
idea: Information theory says only unpredicted bits must cross a channel. Run identical stride/context/value predictors on both sides of the memory link; the sender transmits a 1-bit hit flag when the receiver's prediction is right and an XOR residual otherwise, and both update identically so they stay in lockstep.
why: Regular pointers, zeros and strides could cut bits crossing the interface 2-5x, lowering link pJ and bandwidth demand (facts 5, 8).

title: Fixed-rate ZFP codec in the L2 fill path for simulation arrays
idea: Box: lossy random-access compression × L2 fill/evict path × 4×4×4 float block × fixed 8–16 bits per value × HPC fields. Arrays live in DRAM as fixed-rate ZFP blocks; a cache-side codec decompresses on fill and recompresses on eviction, so code sees plain doubles.
why: HPC mesh size per node is DRAM-bound; 4–8× capacity at error below discretization error.
note: Fixed-rate ZFP in cache fill path is plausible for HPC; hardware ZFP has prior proposals.

title: Double-blind inventory clearinghouse to kill DRAM bullwhip hoarding
idea: Po: every warehouse is made of glass. A neutral party collects encrypted inventory and order data from DRAM makers, distributors and top buyers and, via secure multiparty computation, publishes only weekly aggregate true-demand and channel-inventory indices (like JODI for oil).
why: Double-ordering and hoarding amplify a ~10-15% supply gap into a 4x price spike; transparency deflates phantom demand and lets fabs plan capacity; attacks effective supply.
note: MPC aggregate indices are feasible; participation incentives are the real hurdle.

title: Apollo core-rope weaver: frozen weights in via-programmed ROM chiplets
idea: Apollo's flight software was literally woven into core-rope ROM. Production model weights that won't change for a year are mask-programmed into dense, multi-bit, stackable via-ROM chiplets on a mature node and co-packaged beside the accelerator. HBM then holds only KV cache and activations.
why: Weights are 50-80% of inference HBM. ROM needs no capacitor, no refresh and no EUV, and it can be made in 28-40 nm US fabs. That frees most HBM for KV cache and attacks capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability.
note: Mature-node ROM cost/bit not clearly below DRAM; win is refresh-free, no EUV, weights out of HBM.

title: Alien measures memory in entropy: sell 'effective GB' modules
idea: Aliens count entropy, not bytes. Memory makers sell CXL modules whose controller does inline ANS/LZ compression, cache-line dedup and zero-page elision, plus fabric-wide dedup of identical pages (model weights, OS images, KV-cache prefixes) across 1,000 hosts. They price per effective GB.
why: Meets the 10x constraint for AI inference fleets: 50-100 replicas hold identical weights and shared prompt prefixes, so pooled dedup plus compression gives ~10x effective bits per physical bit for ~5% controller cost. General workloads honestly see 2-3x.

title: Genome-assembler succinct structures with rank/select engines in controller
idea: From genome assemblers that squeeze terabyte de Bruijn graphs into succinct bitvectors: add hardware rank/select and Elias-Fano decode units to the memory controller so pointer-heavy structures (graphs, tries, inverted indexes, B-tree internals) are stored near entropy size yet traversed in one or two memory accesses per hop.
why: Pointer-rich data is often 5-20x larger than its information content; hardware rank/select makes succinct layouts fast enough for general use, cutting DRAM for indexes and graphs 3-10x.

title: Progressive-JPEG bit-plane memory: fetch only needed precision
idea: Satellite and web imagery stream progressive bit planes so receivers stop when good enough. Store tensors bit-plane-sliced across columns (sign/exponent plane first, then mantissa planes); each read requests only the top N planes and only those columns are sensed and sent.
why: Most inference reads need 2-4 effective bits of a 16-bit value; energy per access scales with planes fetched, ~4-8x lower, ~10x with shared block exponents.

title: Bit-significance stack: MSB planes on clean dies, LSB planes on cheap dies
idea: Shift the unit of placement from the word to the bit-plane along the stack's vertical axis: sign, exponent and high-mantissa planes go to 4 protected dies, low-order planes go to 8 dies running at 1% BER with no ECC, and the base die re-interleaves planes into words on the fly.
why: Two-thirds of bits live on refresh-relaxed, low-voltage dies (facts 3, 10) with <0.1% model-quality loss; precision-on-demand fetching also cuts data moved up to ~50%.

title: LLNL ZFP arrays, fixed: lossy compression as a page attribute
idea: ZFP fixed-rate lossy floating-point compression saw low adoption because codes had to be rewritten around compressed-array classes. Put a ZFP engine in the memory controller and let the OS mark pages 'fp64 lossy, 16 bits/value', so unmodified HPC codes get 4x compression with bounded error.
why: ~4x effective DRAM for simulation fields, so HPC nodes need far less DRAM.

title: Vacuum pack with crash foam: compress pages, fill freed space with ECC
idea: Packers shrink-wrap a product and fill the leftover box space with foam. Each 4 KB page in the compressed tier is compressed, and the freed bytes hold a long LDPC/BCH code sized to the space left over. At page scale, 1% raw BER needs about 15-23% parity, so any page that compresses 1.3x or better carries its own armor at no capacity cost. Incompressible pages go to a small protected tier.
why: Flaky 1%-BER cells deliver DRAM-grade reliability for the roughly 70% of pages that compress, with net capacity still about 1.6x thanks to the compression.

title: Factory seconds: sell test-reject DRAM dies as AI-grade memory
idea: Outlet stores sell slightly flawed 'seconds'. DRAM makers take dies that fail JEDEC retention or defect screens but run at about 1% raw BER under relaxed refresh, and bin them into an 'AI-grade' SKU: CXL modules with a page-level LDPC controller, sold for error-tolerant data such as KV, activations and low bit-planes.
why: Recovers the 5-15% of dies that are scrapped or down-binned and lets marginal process windows ship, adding usable bit supply without a new fab at a lower cost per GB.
note: Relaxed-spec AI-grade SKU could widen process windows; needs maker buy-in.

title: Fettling attention: grind off flip burrs from KV before softmax
idea: Foundry fettling grinds the burrs off sand castings. The KV cache lives in 1%-BER cells as int4, with per-head scales protected. The attention kernel 'fettles' each key and value it loads by clamping it to calibrated per-channel bounds and capping softmax weights (top-k trimmed), so a flip that creates an outlier logit cannot hijack attention.
why: Moves the KV cache, the biggest inference memory consumer, to cheap low-refresh cells. int4 already gives 4x capacity, and robust aggregation is expected to keep perplexity within about 0.1-0.3 at 1% BER.
note: Ranger-style range clamping applied to KV in 1%-BER cells.

title: Compiler swaps pointer structures for succinct ones with rank/select instructions
idea: IFR: indexes sized at the information-theoretic minimum. Closest: a profile-guided compiler pass replaces read-mostly maps, sets and trees with succinct equivalents (Elias-Fano, wavelet trees, compressed tries) backed by new rank/select instructions.
why: 2-5x footprint cut for indexes and graphs in search, ads and genomics.

title: Traversal descriptors replace command-address pins entirely
idea: Scarcity: zero command/address pins. The host writes a compact traversal program (base, strides, gather-index pointer, tile shape) into a sequencer in the memory base die once; memory then streams data in consumption order with only a 1-bit flow-control backchannel.
why: Frees ~25-30% of interface pins for data and removes CA energy; the sequencer sees the whole access pattern and orders activations to cut fact-8 page overfetch 2-4x on tensor workloads.
note: Memory-side stream sequencer; poor fit for irregular access.

title: Swap fp16 attention keys for product-quantized codes scored by lookup
idea: Substitute arithmetic on dequantized keys with table lookups. Each cached key becomes 8-16 one-byte product-quantization codes; at decode the query builds a small sub-vector dot-product table, and scores are summed from lookups over the codes, while values use 2-4-bit group quantization. This runs on existing GPUs and unchanged HBM.
why: Shrinks the KV cache 6-10x and the bytes read per token similarly (fact 5), so the same HBM serves several times more context.
note: PQCache-like prior art.

title: Aviation dissimilar redundancy: cross-vendor ECC words
idea: Adapted from fly-by-wire systems that use dissimilar processors from different vendors so one design flaw cannot fail every channel: each ECC codeword in a module or CXL pool is assembled from dies of at least three different vendors or process lots, so a vendor-specific weakness (a hammer-sensitive layout, a lot-wide retention excursion) can hit only one symbol.
why: Row hammer and correlated failures (facts 3, 9): chipkill assumes independent dies, but real failures cluster by vendor and lot; dissimilar assembly makes existing ECC far stronger in practice and lets riskier lower-bin parts fill each slot.
note: Dissimilar-lot codeword assembly decorrelates failures; proof needs fleet failure data.

title: Battery cell matching: retention-matched rank assembly
idea: Adapted from EV battery packs, which group cells of matched capacity so one weak cell does not limit the pack: dies are binned by measured retention (e.g., 64/128/256 ms classes) on existing testers, modules are assembled only from same-class dies, and the class is written to SPD so the controller sets tREFI per rank instead of for the worst die in a mixed rank.
why: Refresh cost (fact 3): today one weak die forces worst-case refresh on its whole rank; matched ranks let 60-80% of modules run 2-4x longer refresh, cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss with only assembly-flow changes.

title: Eliminate fixed-function reliability: firmware-defined, fleet-learned refresh and ECC subscription
idea: Ship <=400 C BEOL memory modules whose refresh timing, reference levels, ECC codes and remap tables live in updatable controller firmware. The vendor learns drift models from fleet telemetry, pushes updates and sells this as a reliability subscription that raises usable capacity over time.
why: Lets vendors ship early, imperfectly characterized low-thermal-budget memories (as SSD makers do with NAND FTLs) while usable yield keeps improving; faster time-to-market for new memory.

title: Flight-recorder DIMM interposer capturing command history before each error
idea: An aircraft's black box records the minutes before an incident. An FPGA DIMM interposer (two board spins, about $250k) keeps a rolling 1-second ring buffer of ACT/REF commands and temperature. On any corrected or uncorrected ECC event it freezes and dumps the buffer. Deployed on ~200 partner servers within the $1M, it would build the first large dataset linking real flips to real access patterns.
why: Measured distributions of hammer and retention tails, rather than worst-case assumptions, allow right-sized mitigation and refresh margins, possibly a 2x relaxation (facts 3 and 9).

title: Epidemic contact tracing: ECC events trigger blast-radius refresh
idea: Epidemiologists trace and test the contacts of each case. When row r reports a corrected error, controller firmware treats it as a case. It immediately refreshes and scrubs r+-1..+-4 using the physical adjacency map. If more cases appear, it raises local refresh and asks the OS to quarantine (remap) the hot aggressor pages.
why: Free ECC events become hammer and weak-cell sensors (facts 3 and 9), and stop cascades before they reach uncorrectable errors. It needs firmware and a kernel hook only.

title: Grade-B DRAM exchange selling dies with certified error maps
idea: Box [medium: any | access: any | sense: standard | integration: DIMM or CXL | substrate: bulk | fab: existing fabs]. A broker buys dies that fail JEDEC retention or hammer limits, tests each to a signed per-die error map, and sells them to hyperscalers whose controllers load the map to retire rows and set per-bank refresh.
why: Supply: unlocks the 5-15% of output that is scrapped or downbinned today, at ~40% discount.

title: NAND-style bad-block maps let partially-good DRAM dies ship
idea: Worse: scrap or down-bin any die whose repair fuses run out. Flip: ship DRAM with a host-visible bad-mat table, like NAND bad blocks, and sell a nominal 32 Gb die as 30 Gb usable, with the OS or CXL controller simply never mapping dead mats.
why: Yield at leading nodes and in HBM (fact 6, 20-30% yield loss): recovering dies that fail on only a few mats can add 10-20% more sellable bits per wafer without new fabs.
note: Partial-good DRAM sales are old; CXL-mapped bad mats is a modern twist.

title: Data-parallel training: model replicas become each other's ECC
idea: In a 10,000-GPU job, every data-parallel rank holds identical weights. Periodically checksum each 2 MB weight shard, compare checksums across replicas over NVLink or InfiniBand, and repair any mismatched shard by copying it from a majority peer. Local HBM errors are then corrected by replication that already exists.
why: Weights are ~30-50% of training HBM. Cross-replica voting gives TMR-like protection for free and lets weight regions run on weaker dies or relaxed refresh (facts 3, 6).

title: Ink-saver encoding keeps fewest cells in leaky charged state
idea: Like ink-saving fonts that print letters with holes, encode each burst with a low-weight code (e.g., 16b to 18b with per-group inversion) chosen using the die's true-cell/anti-cell map, so as few cells as possible sit in the charged state that leaks; retention failures are nearly all charged-to-discharged.
why: Cuts the population of retention-vulnerable cells by ~30-40%, so the same leakage tail (fact 3) yields fewer failures and refresh can stretch ~1.5x; restore energy drops slightly (fact 10) for ~6-12% capacity cost.

title: Selective-assembly die pairing matches complementary defect maps
idea: Bearing makers measure parts and mate oversized balls with undersized races; record each die's failing and weak-row map at wafer test and pair dies into stacks or ranks whose bad addresses do not overlap, so cheap module-level mirroring or spare sharing covers one die's holes with its partner's good rows.
why: Rescues dies that exceed on-die redundancy (several yield points) and makes cross-die repair nearly free because overlaps are engineered to near zero.

title: Grade-mixed ranks: Reed-Solomon makes one cheap die harmless
