idea: Ideal: any die can be used. Closest: a rank uses symbol-level Reed-Solomon over 10 chips with 2 check chips, which lets one chip per rank be a cheap C-grade die with raw BER ~1e-5 (treated as a known-unreliable symbol) while the module still meets server RAS targets.
why: Supply and cost: absorbs down-binned dies into server modules, lowering module cost ~10-15%.
note: Symbol RS tolerating one C-grade die is straightforward; moderate cost win.

title: Capacitor-hole racetrack: electroplated domain-wall nanowires in DRAM's high-aspect-ratio mold
idea: Etch the standard honeycomb hole lattice (~20 nm diameter at 35-40 nm pitch) in oxide. Instead of conformal ALD electrodes, electroplate a magnetic nanowire up from a seed at the hole bottom, modulating composition (Co-rich/Ni-rich, or thin Cu spacers) every ~60 nm to make pinning notches. Bits are axial domains separated by Bloch-point domain walls, which cylindrical wires carry without the Walker breakdown that slows flat racetracks. A vertical select transistor under each hole (4F2/6F2 vertical-channel style) drives ~30 uA bipolar shift pulses through the wire. A 20 nm MTJ on the planarised top reads the top bit and writes it (STT, or SOT from a top heavy-metal line). Half of each track is shift buffer, giving 10 data bits per 1.3 um hole and 25 per 3 um hole.
why: ~10x (1.3 um holes) to ~25x (3 um holes) bits per 1-beta cell footprint: 4.5-11 Gb/mm2 in principle, or 1-beta density at ~3x larger F with no EUV. Refresh energy goes to zero.
note: 10-25 bits per capacitor hole; doubts: notch electroplating in 20 nm AR-65 holes, shift reliability and heating at ~1e7 A/cm2.

title: Negative-capacitance bitline: electrophysiology's capacitance neutralisation applied to the DRAM sense path
idea: A small amplifier per bitline (or a pre-phase folded into the existing sense amplifier) senses the bitline and drives a feedback capacitor Cf with gain A > 1. That injects a current equal to -Cn*dV/dt, with Cn = (A-1)*Cf. For the 1-2 ns of charge sharing, the bitline's effective capacitance becomes Cbl - Cn; then the neutraliser switches off and the normal latch fires. At Cn/Cbl ~0.7 the cell can shrink 3.3x for the same signal. Amplifier offset is auto-zeroed during precharge.
why: Capacitor height falls from 1.3 um to ~260 nm (Cs 5.4 to 1.1 fF) at Cn/Cbl = 0.7, with the same 512-cell bitline. Cost: ~5-8% more periphery area (one amplifier per bitline) and no change to the array architecture.

title: Leakage decay as built-in recency weighting for analog KV caches
idea: Invert 'charge decay is a failure that refresh must undo' -> make decay part of the math. KV-cache and state-space values are stored as un-refreshed analog charge whose leakage time constant is programmed per bank by body bias, so stored magnitude decays exponentially with token age, implementing the recency weighting (decay gates, ALiBi-like bias) models already learn.
why: Eliminates refresh for the largest AI memory consumer (fact 3) and stores 4-6 analog bits per cell, multiplying effective capacity 4-6x for inference KV caches.

title: Logic-die decoupling capacitors double as on-demand scratch memory
idea: Invert 'storage elements must be dedicated memory cells' -> reuse the capacitors already on every logic die. An accelerator's deep-trench/MIM decap is split into ~50 fF segments with access switches, so idle decap banks act as eDRAM-like scratch when the supply-noise budget allows and revert to decoupling during load surges.
why: ~15% of an 800 mm^2 die at ~500 nF/mm^2 is ~1e9 storable bits (~100+ MB) of near-compute memory with ~zero added wafer area, cutting data-movement energy (fact 5) and DRAM demand.

title: Long-channel thick-oxide gain cell in open-source 130 nm
idea: MAGNIFY channel length ~10x and oxide thickness ~3x on the write device: a 3T gain cell in the open SKY130/GF180 PDKs uses the 5 V thick-oxide transistor as write switch (aA subthreshold leakage) and stores on the read transistor's gate; free or cheap shuttles allow monthly iterations.
why: Retention ~1-10 s vs 64 ms (fact 3) in U.S.-fabbed nodes with near-zero capital; niche embedded DRAM for chiplets.
note: Gain-cell eDRAM in open PDKs already explored; niche.

title: Composite: silicon sense chiplets mass-transferred onto glass DRAM panels
idea: TRIZ #40 Composite: large glass panels carry stacked oxide-TFT DRAM tiers, while all precision sensing lives in 50x50 um silicon sense chiplets placed every few millimetres by micro-LED-style mass transfer (millions per hour) and wired by panel redistribution layers; glass does storage, silicon does amplification.
why: 100x path: panel processing costs ~$100-300/m2 versus ~$100k/m2 for EUV DRAM wafers, so with ~0.3 um panel nanoimprint and 16-32 TFT tiers it aims at ~$0.1-0.5/GB; trade-offs: bulky modules, ~us latency and higher energy. Speculative because panel lithography must improve ~5x. Attacks Facts 4 and 7.
note: Multi-tier oxide-TFT DRAM on cheap glass with silicon sense chiplets could hit >10x cost/bit; panel lithography, overlay, us latency doubtful.

title: Rescue rejected DRAM dies behind a strong-ECC buffer controller
idea: Box: existing dies x existing access x existing SA x ECC buffer chip on module x existing substrate x existing fabs. Buy dies that fail JEDEC bins with <=1% bad bits at scrap prices and package them on modules or CXL cards whose buffer chip runs LDPC plus remapping, sold as a new grade.
why: Usable supply rises right away (recapturing yield loss of a few to 10%) with zero new fabs; cost per bit down.

title: Gleaner's cool tier: sense-marginal dies for liquid-cooled racks
idea: Farmers glean the field after harvest. Dies that fail sense margin only above ~75 C are binned as cool-tier DDR5/HBM, sold at standard JEDEC timings into liquid- and immersion-cooled racks that hold devices under 60 C.
why: Turns marginal yield loss into salable bits (+3-8% supply), exploiting how leakage and offset tighten when cool (fact 3).

title: Token-ring wordline sequencer for append-only KV-cache mats
idea: KV-caches append and stream tokens in order, so dedicated mats replace the row decoder with a token passed along a chain of shift-register stages (one per 8 wordlines plus a 3-bit local predecoder), allowing random access only at block granularity. Everything is drawn at DUV pitch.
why: Row-decoder area -60% in AI-tier mats with no EUV-pitch decoders, matched to KV-cache access patterns.

title: Wired-NOR zero-detect lines suppress all-zero bursts at sense stripes
idea: Satellites downlink only non-trivial data: each SA group pulls down a wired-NOR line if any latched bit is 1, so all-zero 64-byte sectors return a 1-bit flag instead of a full burst over global I/O and pins. Sparse AI activations and zero-padded KV pages benefit most.
why: I/O energy (fact 5) down 20-50% on sparse data with trivial DUV circuitry.

title: Predictive-coding memory link transmitting only prediction errors
idea: The visual cortex sends mostly prediction errors, not raw images. Identical lightweight predictors (last-value, stride, zero-run) sit at both ends of a CXL/DIMM link on FPGA, and only the entropy-coded XOR residual crosses the wire. FPGA prototype, ~$600k in 18 months.
why: Fact 5: residuals are mostly zeros, so ~1.5-2x fewer bits cross a 10-20 pJ/bit link. That buys effective bandwidth and energy and lets fewer channels feed the same compute.

title: 3D-NAND toolset builds channel-hole gain cells with no EUV
idea: Ideal: density from tier count with tools already paid for. Closest: in a NAND-style oxide/word-plate stack, each channel hole holds two concentric ALD oxide-semiconductor devices per tier: an outer write channel charging an isolated metal ring, and an inner read channel gated by that ring, so every tier crossing is a capacitorless 2T gain cell built with the 3D NAND etch, ALD and staircase flow.
why: Facts 2 and 4: 100+ tiers at DUV pitch in existing NAND fabs with no capacitor and no EUV; bit cost could follow NAND-like layer economics if speed and retention hold.
note: Concentric write/read oxide devices per channel hole gives NAND-like layer economics; doubt: IGZO speed, ring isolation, retention at tier pitch.

title: Smoke detector: radioisotope micro-battery keeps low-leakage cells alive for decades
idea: Random stimulus 'smoke detector' (a tiny Am-241 source runs for decades) -> a Ni-63 or tritium betavoltaic cell in the module package supplies microwatts forever, refreshing an ultra-low-leakage gain-cell array whose retention is ~1000 s. Data survives loss of external power for ~decades with no new memory material.
why: Non-volatility comes from the package, with zero new process modules or fab capex. At 1000 s retention, refresh for a 16 Gb die is ~0.7 uW, which is within betavoltaic output, and the array keeps DRAM-class speed and unlimited endurance.
note: Package isotope keeps a 1000 s gain-cell array alive; doubts are periphery standby leakage and isotope regulation.

title: 77-kelvin DRAM: crude poly-Si transistors hold charge for hours
idea: Box: MIM charge x solid-phase-crystallized poly-Si TFT (leaky at 300 K) x voltage sense amp x 2D x glass or Si x PECVD a-Si plus furnace crystallization. At 77 K off-current falls by >1e6, so grain-boundary-limited TFTs from a low-mask university flow meet retention for liquid-nitrogen-cooled racks.
why: Uses temperature to relax process quality (no single-crystal Si, no EUV-grade junctions) and nearly removes refresh; LN2 cooling overhead is a few W per W; risk is system-level cryo adoption.
note: Grain-boundary trap-assisted leakage may not fall 1e6 at 77 K; easy university test.

title: Thermophoretic wafer shielding allows ISO-7 cleanrooms for DRAM fabs
idea: Effect: thermophoresis. Every exposed wafer is held 10-20 K warmer than the gas around it inside sealed carriers and tool mini-environments; the thermophoretic force pushes sub-100 nm particles away from the warm surface, cutting deposition velocity by more than 100x, so the ballroom can be ISO 7 instead of ISO 3-4.
why: Capital: cleanroom and facilities are ~20-30% of a $15B fab and a large energy load; a cheaper shell could save billions and about a year of U.S. fab construction.

title: Airbnb for idle cleanroom tools: memory prototyping by the hour
idea: Borrowed from Airbnb monetizing spare rooms: a 10-person team builds a booking, recipe-transfer and wafer-logistics platform over idle tool hours in U.S. university, national-lab and 200 mm commercial cleanrooms, so memory startups route split lots across ALD at one site, etch at another and test at a third.
why: Capital and time: a new cell concept today needs a ~$50M pilot line; renting tool hours gives 10-50x cheaper, faster learning cycles on U.S. soil.

title: Certified pre-owned DRAM: re-profiled hyperscaler memory with warranty
idea: Borrowed from certified pre-owned cars: a 10-person shop buys DIMMs from retired cloud servers by the ton, runs 48-hour retention, row-hammer and temperature profiling on FPGA test rigs, rewrites each DIMM's SPD with measured timing and refresh bins, swaps weak chips and sells warrantied modules for CXL memory expanders.
why: Supply: millions of DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs retire yearly; reuse adds supply with zero wafer capacity at ~30-50% of new price.

title: Minify tier thickness to 6 nm for 1000-tier atomic stacks
idea: Grow alternating MOCVD 2D-semiconductor channel sheets (MoS2 or WSe2, about 1 nm) and hBN/oxide spacers (about 5 nm) so each tier is 6 nm and 1000 tiers fit in a 6 um stack. Gain-cell storage nodes are gated by shared vertical gate holes etched once per 100-tier deck, as in 3D NAND.
why: 3D break-even (26+ tiers): goes 40x past it at a stack height that an etcher can already reach; the wide bandgap of 2D channels also cuts leakage, so refresh could fall by more than 100x.
note: 1000 tiers at 6 nm pitch would be far past 10x density; doubt: sequential 2D growth/transfer yield.

title: Band-offset quantum-well bits stacked along a superlattice pillar
idea: Worse: store each bit on a bulky capacitor needing femtofarads. Flip: etch vertical pillars through a Si/Ge-rich superlattice, wrap each Ge-rich well with a tier gate, and store holes in its valence-band well (up to ~0.5 eV offset) as the bit, sensed as a threshold shift of the shared vertical Si channel, which is capacitorless and has no oxide tunneling, so endurance stays unlimited.
why: Every tier of every pillar is a bit: 128 tiers at 50 nm pillar pitch is ~17 nm2/bit (~50x), so 10x survives even at 20% array efficiency with NAND-like process cost; retention from thermal emission over the band offset is the speculative part.
note: Capacitorless bit per tier gives ~50x density; doubt: 0.5 eV offset means ~us retention at 85C, not ms.

title: Wafer-scale DRAM bonded under a wafer-scale accelerator replaces HBM
idea: Substitute HBM stacks plus interposer with one full DRAM wafer hybrid-bonded face-to-face to a wafer-scale processor: each compute tile gets the DRAM directly beneath it through ~2 um-pitch bonds, and defective DRAM tiles are routed around by the processor's existing redundancy fabric.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): ~3-4 pJ/bit -> <0.3 pJ/bit and >10x bandwidth per mm², with no TSVs (fact 6) and no reticle-limited interposer.
note: ~10x lower pJ/bit and TB-class capacity under compute; doubts: accelerator heat on DRAM retention, matching redundancy.

title: Oxygen: porous-silicon oxidation carves many SOI tiers from one epi stack
idea: Grow an epi stack alternating p+ (~1e19) and lightly doped Si, open slits, anodize in HF so only the p+ layers become mesoporous, then oxidize them at ~850 C into buried oxide (FIPOS); the lightly doped layers remain single-crystal device tiers.
why: Crystalline multi-tier SOI with no germanium (no SiGe mismatch limit on tier count) and no bonding cycles; attacks the lateral-transistor blocker (fact 2) at epi-reactor cost.
note: Porous-Si oxidation (FIPOS) carves many crystalline tiers without SiGe strain limits; boron diffusion and expansion stress are risks.

title: Potassium hydroxide on (110) silicon etches crystal-perfect vertical cell walls
idea: Align lines along <112> on (110) Si and etch in KOH so the slow {111} planes form atomically smooth vertical walls 20-40 nm thick at >100:1 aspect ratio; a deposited oxide/TiN wordline stack crossing the walls turns each wall into a vertical string of DRAM cells.
why: Single-crystal vertical semiconductor sheets for stacked cells (fact 2) without DRIE or EUV (fact 4), from a heated beaker; smooth walls trim the interface-trap leakage tail (fact 3).
note: Ultra-high-AR {111} KOH walls are proven in MEMS; novel as DRAM channel sheets, but capacitor placement is unaddressed.

title: Vertical charge-coupled memory: no switch per bit, just moving charge
idea: Inverts 'every bit needs its own access transistor': deposit a 200-layer gate/oxide stack (NAND-style, one hole etch), line each hole with a poly-Si or oxide channel, and clock the layer gates in 3 phases so charge packets march along the hole like a vertical CCD. Each hole holds ~60 bits and one sense/regeneration stage at the top restores packets as they circulate, so refresh is continuous and free.
why: No per-bit transistor, capacitor or litho: cost tracks 3D NAND (~$0.05-0.1/GB), ~100x below DRAM per GB; trade-off is serial access (~us to the far bit, high streaming bandwidth) and transfer-loss risk in poly channels.
note: CCD clocking in a NAND-style stack removes per-bit transistors and capacitors; poly-channel transfer efficiency and serial latency are the doubts.

title: Image-sensor pinned-photodiode storage node with a transfer gate
idea: Adapted from the CMOS image sensor's pinned photodiode: store the bit as electrons in a fully depleted buried n-well capped by a p+ pinning layer, isolated from every Si/SiO2 interface, and move it to a floating diffusion through a transfer gate. A source follower reads it like a 4T pixel, so ~1-3k electrons suffice instead of ~30k.
why: Pinned photodiodes reach dark currents of a few electrons per second (~aA) at room temperature, ~10^4x below the 13 fA tail (fact 3); retention of seconds nearly removes refresh and the need for a 60-75:1 capacitor (fact 1), at 3-4 transistors per cell.
note: Pinned wells cut dark current hugely, but 3-4T pixel-like cells are far larger than 6F2; demoable on CIS MPW.

title: Antiferroelectric latent-charge buffer holds stored-1 voltage on a plateau
idea: Reverse the capacitor dielectric's role from passive to defending its charge: use ZrO2-rich antiferroelectric HZO and bias the plate so a stored '1' sits just above the AFE back-switching voltage. As leakage drains the node, AFE domains switch back and release bound polarization charge (~10-20 uC/cm2), pinning the voltage on a plateau the way latent heat holds ice water at 0 C.
why: Retention and charge wall (facts 1, 3): effective capacitance at the hold point rises 5-10x, so retention rises ~5x without taller pillars; AFE has no remanent polarization, avoiding the fatigue/imprint of prior HZO FeRAM concepts.
note: AFE back-switching plateau multiplies effective hold capacitance; AFE endurance far below 1e15 and nm-scale domain granularity are doubts.

title: Image-sensor 4T pixel gain cell reads 1,000-electron packets
idea: Box: buried-channel storage well (~1-2k e-) x transfer gate + floating-diffusion source follower borrowed from 4T image pixels x correlated-double-sampling column sensing x planar CMOS x Si x CIS fab flow. Full charge transfer onto a tiny floating diffusion gives ~100 uV/e- gain, so a small well replaces the 5 fF capacitor and is written back after read.
why: Escapes the capacitor charge wall (fact 1); buried-channel wells with CIS-grade dark current (few e-/s) extend retention 10-100x (fact 3); reuses existing CIS fab capacity.
note: CIS pinned wells give ~e-/s dark current; doubt is density (~1 um pixels) and transfer speed; CIS MPW demo feasible.

title: Float-glass style liquid-gallium printing of atomically thin Ga2O3 channels
idea: As float glass forms on molten tin, kiss the wafer against a liquid Ga/In alloy. Its self-limiting 1.5-3 nm oxide skin transfers at room temperature as a crystalline wide-gap 2D channel for BEOL access transistors.
why: Eg ~4.8 eV in an atomically thin channel could push off-current below 1e-21 A per cell (beyond IGZO). It is BEOL-stackable for 3D with no epitaxy tool, aiming for >100x less refresh.
note: Room-temperature transfer of Ga2O3 skin from liquid metal as BEOL channel; wafer-scale uniformity and contacts are open.

title: Legacy-node always-on island lets modern DRAM fully power down
idea: Put a 32-64 MB refresh-free die on the package (180 nm thick-oxide or loadless cells) holding page tables, kernel and wake state. Modern DRAM banks then enter deep power-down with no refresh when idle, flushing or discarding their contents.
why: Idle refresh power (16-33%) goes to near zero for phones and lightly loaded servers, and U.S. legacy fabs make the island.

title: Papermaker's book: roll-to-roll foil memory laminated 800 sheets deep
idea: A papermaker makes thick books from cheap sheets. Print single-tier oxide-TFT gain-cell memory on 10 um polyimide foil by roll-to-roll nanoimprint at ~100 nm rules, then laminate ~800 sheets per cm with anisotropic conductive film and edge-plated through-stack bus lines into a memory 'book'.
why: Meets the 10x constraint volumetrically: ~60 MB/cm^2 per sheet times 800 sheets is ~50 GB/cm^3, versus ~2 GB/cm^3 for a DIMM. Roll-to-roll costs (~$20-50/m^2 per sheet) keep cost per module flat; sheet alignment and yield are the risks.
note: If 800 laminated R2R TFT sheets yield, cost/GB falls >10x; sheet yield, alignment and through-stack interconnect are near-miraculous.

title: Main memory inside the logic die's own metal stack (monolithic BEOL oxide gain cells)
idea: After the logic metal stack is complete (TSMC has already embedded an oxide-semiconductor-selector memory fully in BEOL above advanced logic), deposit 8-16 tiers of vertical IGZO/ZTO 2T0C cells with 3 bits/cell write-verify, local complementary-oxide sensing (B2-08) and short vias down to SRAM-buffered memory controllers. Oxide cells retain >200 s at 95 C, so they tolerate sitting on hot logic. On backside-power logic, the frontside BEOL is less congested. Capacity is the target, not cache: an 800 mm2 die area carries 76-152 GB.
why: 76-152 GB over an 800 mm2 die (3 b x 8-16 tiers at F=40 nm, no EUV); interface energy 3.5 -> ~0.2 pJ/bit, saving 211-422 W per accelerator at 8-16 TB/s; zero extra wafers; added cost ~$0.87/GB at $500 per tier per wafer and 80% yield.
note: Capacity-class (76-152 GB) memory in logic BEOL at ~0.2 pJ/bit; doubt: 3-bit oxide MLC stability on hot logic and BEOL yield.

title: Nested-precision bit-plane memory + self-speculative decoding
idea: INT8/FP8 weights are quantised in a nested (Matryoshka-style) way, so the top 2 or 4 bit planes are themselves a usable low-precision model. The memory controller stores the planes in separate address ranges and streams 'planes 0-1', 'planes 0-3' or all of them, in 512 B-2 KB chunks that match DRAM bursts and pages. Decode is self-speculative: draft k tokens with the top planes only (25-50% of the weight bytes), then verify all k in one batched pass with every plane. No second model is stored.
why: 1.1-1.8x effective decode bandwidth (weight reads per accepted token 0.89-0.55), with zero extra capacity.

title: Vertical oxide CCD string: transistor-less 3D charge-shift memory
idea: Etch one high-aspect-ratio hole through 128-256 alternating W/Mo and SiO2 word planes (the same module as 3D NAND), and line it with a thin gate oxide and an ALD IGZO/IGO channel. Clock planes in 4 phases (2 gates per bit): each bit is a packet of ~1,000-5,000 electrons in an accumulation well. Si CCDs lose stored charge to thermal generation (dark current); wide-gap IGZO generates essentially no carriers, so packets hold, limited only by inter-well barriers and gate leakage. Reading shifts packets out of the top of the string into a charge-transfer sense amp (B1-04) on bonded periphery, and data recirculates to the bottom: a delay-line memory with 32-64-bit strings and thousands of parallel holes per line access. Planes are segmented into small blocks to keep plane RC at ~1 ns per phase.
why: 4.2-8.3x 1b density (1.85-3.7 Gb/mm2 at 128-256 planes) with zero per-bit devices; streaming read energy 17-67 fJ/bit; but access is serial (32-128 ns worst-case to a given bit).
note: Transistor-less charge-shift strings on NAND tooling; doubts: IGZO trap states hurting transfer efficiency, and serial access latency.

title: Nanogap (vacuum/air) tunnel-barrier floating node: flash-like retention without oxide wear
idea: The floating metal node (TiN or W, anchored on dielectric on one side) faces a write electrode across a 2.5-4 nm gap. The gap is made by removing an ALD sacrificial layer (carbon or Al2O3) and then sealed, like BEOL air-gaps or NASA's nanoscale vacuum-channel transistors, which work in air because the gap is far below the ~70 nm mean free path. The node is the gate of an IGZO or Si read transistor (2T-like gain cell), so the read is non-destructive. Writing uses field emission at a few V/nm (field enhancement 2-3 at edges); holding relies on the exponential non-linearity of tunnelling. Charge never passes through a solid dielectric, so there are no trap generation, SILC or charge-to-breakdown limits, the mechanisms that cap flash endurance at ~1e5. Low-work-function coatings (LaB6-class, 2.7 eV) cut write voltage, but even plain TiN (4.5 eV) works at 8 V.
why: [SPECULATIVE] A non-volatile, refresh-free DRAM-class gain cell: retention 3.7e4 s (2.5 nm gap, 2.7 eV) to >1e8 s (3 nm), writes in 0.4-40 ns. Endurance is not set by oxide damage, with a target of >=1e12.
note: Charge never crosses a solid dielectric, removing oxide-wear endurance limits; doubt: sealing reproducible 2.5-4 nm gaps given exponential gap sensitivity.

title: Coolant-backed memory wafer: microchannels in the memory layer of a memory-on-logic stack
idea: In a face-to-face memory-on-logic stack (B3-02, or any bonded DRAM-over-logic), etch 100-200 um deep microchannels into the back of the thick memory wafer, away from its devices, and run warm water through them. The memory devices then sit only ~50 um of silicon plus their own BEOL from the coolant, while the logic's heat crosses the memory on its way out. With in-silicon microchannels of the kind Microsoft and Corintis demonstrated in 2025, the memory layer runs ~9-28 K above coolant instead of at the 70-105 C of a cold-plate GPU junction. DRAM retention roughly doubles for every 10 C drop, so a Si 1T1C array at ~45 C holds a 64 ms tail cell for ~1 s.
why: Refresh energy and refresh busy-time 8-16x lower for ordinary Si DRAM (64 ms -> 0.5-1 s; 7.6% -> 0.5-0.9% of time), and standard DRAM becomes viable directly on 1 kW logic without switching to oxide cells.

title: Vt-coded in-stack tier decoder: kill the staircase so 3D DRAM lines can be short
idea: 3D NAND reaches each tier's horizontal line through a staircase whose length grows with tier count; DRAM wants short lines (sub-page activation, low RC), and at 64 tiers a ~32 um staircase is longer than a 512-cell line. Instead, route every tier's horizontal line under 2*log2(N) vertical select-gate pillars before it merges into one common vertical contact. In each tier, each select region is permanently depletion-mode (always on) or enhancement-mode according to that tier's binary address, so driving the pillars with an address and its complement opens exactly one tier's path. The code is written per tier during deposition with one coarse (um-scale, i-line) block mask, or, as in Macronix-style LSM for 3D NAND, by programming charge-trap select gates once at test.
why: Line-termination area 12x smaller at 64 tiers (32 um staircase -> 2.7 um) and 21x at 128; line-end overhead for a 128-cell line 83% -> 30%, enabling 4x shorter wordlines and correspondingly less activation overfetch.

title: Yield firewall: spare tiers per block plus pre-tested tier groups
idea: Build 64 + s tiers per block and fuse out up to s defective tiers per block through the tier decoder (B3-08 makes tier selection programmable), so one killer defect in one tier no longer kills a block. For very tall stacks, build tiers in groups of 8 on separate carriers, run parametric tests on each group (vertical-bitline continuity, leakage, Vt maps from built-in test structures), and stack only good groups by die-to-wafer hybrid bonding. That turns a multiplicative 64-tier yield into a sum of 8-tier yields plus bond yields.
